headline: Monday market brief: Friday selloff meets a pre-open US session and fresh data tests
overview: As of the 13:00 London cutoff on Monday, November 2, London is 13:00 GMT and New York is 08:00 EST; the NYSE core session is scheduled for 09:30–16:00 ET and has not opened, so no November 2 US equity close exists. Friday October 30 is the latest completed US equity session. The report carries forward dated evidence on the AI-led selloff, rates, inflation, commodities, housing and international activity, and sets concrete tests for the Monday open and this week’s releases.

items.headline: Friday US stocks closed lower as AI valuation worries deepened
items.detail: AP reported on October 30 that technology shares led a broad US selloff as investors questioned whether AI spending and valuations had run too far. Friday was a completed NYSE session; Monday’s cash session is not yet open, so no November 1 close exists.
items.why: The close is a measured risk repricing; it does not prove a durable change in AI demand. The next test is whether breadth and credit conditions stabilize when US trading resumes.
items.watch: Compare Monday opening breadth and megacap earnings follow-through with Friday’s close.

sources.title: US stocks closed lower as AI valuations were questioned

items.headline: US futures are slightly higher before the NYSE open
items.detail: AP reported on October 27 that US futures edged higher after an AI-led Wall Street rally, while global shares were mixed ahead of major earnings and central-bank decisions. At the 12:58 UTC cutoff New York was 08:58 ET, before the 09:30 ET NYSE open, so no October 27 cash move is available.
items.why: The gap between futures and the eventual cash open matters because overnight prices can reverse once US liquidity and company-specific earnings arrive. Friday’s close is the completed reference point; Monday breadth and the close remain unavailable at this cutoff.
items.watch: Compare the 09:30 ET open, breadth and the October 27 close with the pre-open futures reading.

items.headline: Treasuries rallied as investors sought safety
items.detail: AP reported October 30 that Treasury yields sank as investors sought safer assets during the technology selloff, while BLS reported compensation costs rose 0.8% in Q3. This dated observation should be read alongside the next release and subsequent market response, because one session cannot establish a lasting trend.
items.why: Lower yields can ease duration pressure, but firm labor costs may keep inflation risk alive. The combination leaves the curve dependent on whether growth or inflation dominates the next data.
items.watch: Check two-year and ten-year yields after the November jobs report and next inflation release.

items.headline: The Fed decision is tomorrow, not today
items.detail: AP’s October 27 preview says investors see almost no chance of an October hike after officials downplayed the likelihood, while the policy rate is about 3.9%. The October 28 decision is now a dated reference point; the next test is the November policy and data sequence.
items.why: The outcome is more than the rate itself: language on inflation, oil and longer-term yields can reset the path priced into equities and credit. Treating an expected hold as a delivered decision would overstate the evidence.
items.watch: Compare the actual statement, press conference and two-year yield reaction on October 28.

items.headline: Next week’s US data calendar will test the soft landing narrative
items.detail: The Bureau of Labor Statistics schedule lists Job Openings and Labor Turnover for September on November 3, productivity and costs for Q3 on November 5, and the October Employment Situation on November 6 at 08:30 ET. These are scheduled releases, not results; Monday’s US cash-market print is not yet available.
items.why: A labor-demand reading followed by productivity and payroll data can change the balance between growth resilience and inflation pressure in rates and equities. The calendar gives investors a dated test without pretending the data is already known.
items.watch: Read JOLTS on November 3, productivity on November 5 and payrolls on November 6 against Treasury yields and market breadth.

items.headline: UK surveys and spending diverge before the budget
items.detail: Reuters reported that the preliminary October UK composite PMI rose to 53.1 from September’s 52.0, while September retail sales weakened. Sterling reached a seventeen-month high against the euro on Friday October 23. The October 28 UK budget is still pending.
items.why: Stronger business surveys and softer household spending give different signals for growth and tax capacity. The budget will test whether fiscal choices add support without reigniting gilt or inflation concerns under expensive energy.
items.watch: Read the October 28 budget measures and compare sterling and gilt yields with Friday’s levels.

items.headline: German confidence improves but current conditions weaken
items.detail: The October 26 ifo survey showed Germany’s business climate at 90.2, up from 89.9 in September, according to Reuters. Expectations climbed to 91.6 from 90.4, while current conditions fell to 88.8 from 89.5. The ECB decision is due later this week.
items.why: The divergence suggests firms see a better six-month outlook without a present demand rebound. Higher energy costs and French sovereign stress could still tighten financing conditions across the euro area.
items.watch: Compare the October ifo split with flash inflation, GDP and Thursday’s ECB communication.

items.headline: Oil import bill leaves Japan exposed before BoJ meeting
items.detail: Japan’s finance ministry data released October 21 showed an April-to-September trade deficit of 2.81 trillion yen, AP reported. September alone was a 536.6 billion yen deficit, the fifth consecutive monthly shortfall, as oil imports became more expensive. This is dated carry-forward evidence.
items.why: Higher import costs can weaken the yen and lift domestic prices even while export volumes grow. The Bank of Japan must judge whether inflation is persistent enough to justify further tightening without deepening pressure on activity.
items.watch: Read this week’s Bank of Japan decision and the next trade and inflation releases.
